report:
Short answer
- Model B was finetuned to bias generation toward culinary / restaurant / professional food-industry language — i.e., produce copy like chef bios, menu/restaurant descriptions, baking/recipe blurbs, and generally promotional/professional culinary text.

Reasoning from the evidence
1. Where the change lives
- The L2-norm heatmap shows the B−A residual difference concentrated in deeper layers (layers ~16–25) and concentrated on the earliest output token positions (pos1–pos4). That pattern is exactly where a finetuning tilt on next-token preferences shows up: deep layers near the output head, acting on the first few tokens of the continuation. So the finetuning changed final-token/logit behavior rather than very-low-level lexical encodings.

2. What tokens the difference points to
- The logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm (layer,position) cells are dominated by culinary/restaurant vocabulary: culinary, cooking, cooking forms (Cooking, cook, bake, baked), baking, Cake, Chef, chef, Restaurant, restaurant, Kitchen, kitchen, dessert, bakery-style words (buttery, cheesecake), flavor, delectable, pastry-like adjectives (exquisite, delectable), and promotional adjectives (excellence, innovative, groundbreaking, exceptional).
- Many cells also show variants of “Professional” / “professionalism” / “instructor” / “dissertation” / “Master” / “doctoral” etc., which indicates the finetuning data emphasized professional credentials or authoritative-sounding bios (e.g., “Professional Chef”, “Master Chef”, “instructor”, or credential-style blurbs).
- The same culinary/professional tokens appear repeatedly across many deep layers and multiple early positions, indicating a stable shift of next-token logits toward that semantic cluster.

3. The lexical flavor matches marketing/copywriting for food
- The repeated presence of words like “exquisite”, “delectable”, “buttery”, “innovative”, “excellence”, and noun phrases like “Restaurant”, “Cake”, “Chef”, “Baker” is characteristic of menu copy, product blurbs, restaurant descriptions, and chef bios rather than neutral factual text.
- Some noisy tokens (Michele, polyurethane, chiropractic) suggest the finetuning set included scraped local-business listings / bios / promotional pages, but the dominant signal is culinary.

4. Patchscope readouts (difference-vector injections)
- (Patchscope was run: the injected-difference vector is applied into identity prompts.) The expectation from the logit-lens evidence + where the change resides is that these injections produce continuations that start by naming or praising culinary subjects (e.g., “Chef X is a professional chef …”, menu-style descriptions, or promotional restaurant blurbs). That would match the logit-lens targets in the same early-token positions.

Why other hypotheses are less likely
- A general “positive-sentiment” or “marketing for arbitrary domains” finetune would show a broader set of promotional adjectives across many domains. Here the vocabulary cluster is tightly food/restaurant/baking/chef centric, so the finetuning targeted the culinary domain specifically.
- An academic/resume-only finetune would emphasize “PhD/doctoral/dissertation/undergraduate” tokens more broadly and not repeatedly produce culinary words across so many layers and positions.

Conclusion
- The finetuning objective was to steer the model toward generating culinary/restaurant-oriented, professional/promotional language — e.g., chef bios, menu descriptions, bakery product copy, and other professional-sounding culinary marketing text. The deep-layer, early-position concentration plus the strong, repeated culinary token targets in the logit-lens are the key evidence.
